intro: Clouds move, but the sky does not travel towards a destination. Debussy lets rocking chords and a recurring cor anglais phrase drift around a B-centred background; a lighter flute-and-harp passage briefly changes the illumination. The third movement, Sirènes, is not included here because the women’s chorus in this recording has not been fully identified.
question: Can a returning colour make a form as clearly as a returning tune?

sections.label: B · A brighter clearing

cues.title: Motion without a destination
cues.text: Across the opening, clarinets and bassoons rock between quiet chords rather than launch a tune with a clear destination. Listen for this repeated motion as a background against which a more individual phrase can emerge.
cues.evidence: Viewed original orchestral score, Indiana/Kalmus reprint, p. 2, and Jobert 1930 p. 1: rocking clarinet and bassoon quarters. Analysis begins at a low relative level, −28.4 dB in the 0–5 s window. This describes the opening passage, not an aligned first attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A phrase that keeps returning
cues.text: The cor anglais supplies a distinctive, unhurried phrase, set apart from the rocking background. Remember its contour rather than treating it as the beginning of a conventional song: its returns help hold together a scene whose harmony keeps changing shade.
cues.evidence: Jobert score pp. 2–3 gives the cor anglais phrase; original p. 16 later restores it. The report shows a withdrawal around 30–45 s and a novelty peak at 42 s. These locate an early quiet passage, not a precisely detected instrumental entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A title borrowed from painting
cues.text: Here “nocturne” suggests colour and light, not the familiar kind of solo-piano night piece. Debussy’s programme described the title in a decorative sense; Stephen Walsh also connects these orchestral pieces with Whistler’s paintings.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s programme is quoted by the Los Angeles Philharmonic: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes. Stephen Walsh, CMS biography, Middle Period: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/composers/claude-debussy

cues.title: Follow the swell, not a beat count
cues.text: Through this stretch, the quiet surface repeatedly gathers weight and recedes. Follow the span of each swell rather than trying to make every instrumental gesture coincide with an equally strong beat.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −32.3 dB at 100 s to −14.4 dB at 120 s, then retreats by 125–135 s. These are relative-level windows within this file; the report’s onset-based tempo estimate is not used as a musical pulse.

cues.title: Two movements before three
cues.text: Nuages and Fêtes were first performed together in Paris on 9 December 1900, conducted by Camille Chevillard. Sirènes joined them at the first complete performance on 27 October 1901: the three-part work reached the public in two stages.
cues.evidence: IMSLP work catalogue, First Performance entries: https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes_(Debussy,_Claude). The LA Philharmonic note also gives the two premiere dates: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes

cues.title: After the strongest early crest
cues.text: The opening field has just reached a substantial swell and withdrawn. Notice how much activity can remain after the weight has gone: a returning phrase or a small accompanying figure can keep the scene moving without another climax.
cues.evidence: The largest relative-level windows in the file are 165–175 s, followed by a fall to −23.3 dB at 175–180 s and quieter values through 190 s. No instrument or harmonic change is inferred from that measurement.

cues.title: An orchestral language taking shape
cues.text: Debussy composed the Nocturnes in 1897–99, between the orchestral Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and the completion of Pelléas et Mélisande. These works share an interest in suggestion, changing sonority and phrases that need not behave like square-cut songs.
cues.evidence: Stephen Walsh dates the Nocturnes 1897–99, the Prélude 1891–94 and the nine-year composition of Pelléas begun in 1893: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/composers/claude-debussy. The last sentence is an editorial comparison, not a claim of a quotation between works.

cues.title: Listen for a change of light
cues.text: As the first large span approaches its end, keep its dark, repeated gestures in mind. The contrasting middle will not need a grand announcement: a more flowing melody and a different blend of instruments can make the scene feel newly lit.
cues.evidence: Original score pp. 12–13 leads into Un peu animé at rehearsal 7. The report places a low-level window at 265–270 s before a pronounced rise and change around 268–275 s. This is an anticipatory form note, not a claim that the melody starts at 252 s.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Flute and harp, one outline
cues.text: In the middle passage, flute and harp share a melody drawn from five notes, a pentatonic collection. The sustained strings make a quiet background. Compare this flowing outline with the cor anglais phrase: the contrast comes from shape and scoring as well as pitch.
cues.evidence: Viewed original score p. 13, rehearsal 7, and Jobert pp. 12–13: flute and harp double the five-note melody above divided sustained strings. The report’s change at 268 s and contrasting 270–310 s span support this broad placement; no note-level alignment is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first colour comes back
cues.text: Around the return, the cor anglais recovers its familiar phrase and the score restores the original tempo. The earlier material is recognisable, but its thinner surroundings make this a recollection rather than a replay of the whole opening.
cues.evidence: Viewed original p. 16 and Jobert p. 15 mark 1er tempo and restore the cor anglais figure over clarinet/bassoon support, with lower strings joining. The strong novelty peak at 322 s and fall in relative level around 315–325 s anchor the estimated return.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Notice what is being left out
cues.text: In the returning field, listen as much for space as for melody. Sustained lower sounds and short recollections can carry the memory of the opening without rebuilding its full texture; the closing passage will reduce that memory further.
cues.evidence: Jobert pp. 15–16 and original pp. 16–17 thin the return around cor anglais, low strings and soft timpani. The report remains below the middle-section crest through 335–370 s. Timing is provisional and does not identify individual rests.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An ending made by subtraction
cues.text: Towards the close, the score asks for slower motion and breaks the sustained scene into fragments and quiet plucked string sounds. Let the gaps belong to the phrase. The piece disappears instead of assembling a final orchestral declaration.
cues.evidence: Viewed original p. 18 and Jobert p. 17: Plus lent, Encore plus lent, fragmentary wind writing and pizzicato strings. The report becomes especially quiet after 400 s and approaches silence in the 425–431 s tail; the last attack is not precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A new line changes the illumination
transitions.how: The opening’s short gestures give way to a longer flute line doubled by harp. Debussy marks Un peu animé, slightly more animated, and replaces the rocking background with sustained divided strings. The melody uses a five-note collection, while the written key signature moves from two sharps to six. This is a change of harmonic field, motion and orchestral colour, not a forceful cadence announcing a new tune. The low strings sustain rather than drive a new bass progression.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 12–13, rehearsal 7; Jobert pp. 11–12. The report places a novelty peak at 268 s after a very quiet 265–270 s window, with a rise at 270–275 s. These support a provisional passage boundary; the five-note collection and scoring come from the viewed notation, not machine key labels.

transitions.title: The cor anglais restores the first scene
transitions.how: The brighter melody subsides and the cor anglais retrieves its earlier contour. At 1er tempo, the score returns to the opening pace and two-sharp signature. Clarinet and bassoon support reappears; lower strings subsequently sustain near the fingerboard, while the flute-and-harp pairing withdraws. Familiar material therefore returns through an instrumental handover and a thinning texture, not through a triumphant B-minor cadence.
transitions.evidence: Viewed original p. 16 and Jobert pp. 14–15 provide the returning phrase, 1er tempo and sul-tasto lower strings. The report’s strong 322 s novelty peak and lower 315–325 s level support the provisional boundary. No particular returning note is time-aligned.

transitions.title: The phrase becomes scattered remnants
transitions.how: The closing span does not introduce another contrasting theme. Debussy gradually removes the connective tissue: the cor anglais phrase gives way to bassoon, flute and horn fragments, with the instruction Plus lent and later Encore plus lent. Soft timpani and low strings preserve the background before plucked string sounds replace the longer-held texture. The ending is made by reduction and increasing space, rather than by a large cadential progression.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 17–18 and Jobert pp. 16–17. A measured change at 372 s, falling spectral centroid across 370–395 s and the very low 400–431 s tail locate the broad dissolution. The coda boundary is editorial and provisional, not a measured first bar of Plus lent.

timeline.note: Provisional opening map: clarinet and bassoon chords rock quietly; this is the notated starting texture.
Provisional early-passage map: the cor anglais phrase is set against held wind and muted violin colours, with soft timpani.
Provisional broad swell: wind figures and the string field gain weight; this is not an exact tutti entrance.
Provisional withdrawal after the early crest: the characteristic cor anglais gesture is foregrounded above reduced string activity.
Provisional late-opening passage: exposed oboe and viola writing thins the texture before the brighter middle.
Provisional rehearsal-7 passage: flute and harp share the melody over sustained divided strings; clarinet and bassoon add brief replies.
Provisional continuation: solo string lines and muted horn colouring carry the middle span beyond the initial flute-and-harp pairing.
Provisional return: the cor anglais phrase comes back; low strings and wind support enter and withdraw within the passage.
Provisional closing region: the line passes into lower, fragmentary writing above very soft timpani and sustained strings.
Provisional final page: brief wind remnants, timpani and pizzicato strings recede; groups do not all sound continuously.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
